York has a famous one too: York Minster.
It's a place for Sunday services.
questions.fun_fact: Almost every English and British monarch since William the Conqueror in 1066 has been crowned in Westminster Abbey.

media.author: Alan Hunt

questions.description: Kneel down, keep still and try not to sneeze near the sword.
questions.question: In the UK, who has the power to make someone a knight?
hints: This job is passed down through one family.
Each year this person opens Parliament with a speech.
This person lives in palaces such as Buckingham Palace.
questions.fun_fact: The light tap of a sword on each shoulder that makes someone a knight is called the “accolade”.

media.credit: Tony Peake · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tony Peake

questions.description: Someone has tried to sneak into Camelot without a proper invitation.
questions.question: Thomas Malory's 15th-century book “Le Morte d'Arthur” tells of King Arthur's knights. Which of these is NOT a Knight of the Round Table?
hints: The odd one out is a knight, but from a different story.
He comes from a novel written in the 1800s.
Sir Walter Scott wrote about him, in a story set in the time of Richard the Lionheart.
questions.fun_fact: Malory is thought to have written much of “Le Morte d'Arthur” while he was in prison.

media.credit: Bryn Holmes · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bryn Holmes

questions.description: The ultimate wedding present: forget the toaster.
questions.question: In 1152, the future Henry II of England married a former Queen of France, who became the mother of Richard the Lionheart. What land did she bring him?
hints: It lay on the other side of the Channel.
It stretched across the south-west of France.
Bordeaux and its vineyards were part of it.
questions.fun_fact: Eleanor was Queen of France and then Queen of England, lived to about 80 and was also the mother of King John.

media.author: JackyM59

questions.description: He's got Scotland's top job, but he never popped in for a visit.
questions.question: Scotland's patron saint, Andrew, was a fisherman, Saint Peter's brother and one of Jesus's twelve apostles. Where did he come from?
hints: He spent his working days on the water.
He fished on a large lake that is sometimes called a sea.
Nazareth is in the same region.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Saint Andrew's bones were brought to Scotland, and the town of St Andrews is named after him.

media.credit: Bill Harrison · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bill Harrison

questions.description: The medieval version of “just chuck everything in”.
questions.question: I bubbled away over the fire in almost every medieval peasant's home, a thick stew of peas, beans, oats and whatever vegetables were around. What am I?
hints: I was eaten every day, often with bread.
I could stay on the fire for days, with new things added.
My name comes from the pot I was cooked in.
questions.fun_fact: Pease pottage, made from peas, is linked to the old rhyme “Pease porridge hot, pease porridge cold”.

media.credit: TopmanJnr1 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TopmanJnr1

questions.description: Court fashion with a few loose ends.
questions.question: Medieval English kings kept jesters to make them laugh. What hung from the tips of a jester's floppy, pointed hat?
hints: You hear them before you see them.
They made sure everyone noticed when the jester moved his head.
Father Christmas has them on his sleigh.
questions.fun_fact: Some jesters were the only people allowed to make fun of the king without getting into trouble.

media.credit: DeFacto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DeFacto

questions.description: Interior design with a strong hint of “please don't fight”.
questions.question: Front-bench MPs aren't meant to step over these red lines on the Commons floor. They're said to be how many sword lengths apart?
hints: The idea is that no one could reach the other side with a sword.
The rule has to be fair to both sides of the House.
Imagine a sword held out from each side, the tips meeting in the middle.
questions.fun_fact: MPs still have ribbon loops in their cloakroom, meant for hanging up their swords.

questions.description: Two ships went looking for a shortcut and turned up about 170 years late.
questions.question: Sir John Franklin's ships Erebus and Terror vanished in the Arctic in the 1840s. Their wrecks were found in 2014 and 2016, helped by the stories of which people?
hints: They live in the region where the ships disappeared.
Their stories about the lost ships were passed down for generations.
They are the Indigenous people of Arctic Canada and Greenland.
questions.fun_fact: The TV series “The Terror” (2018) retold Franklin's lost expedition, and Inuit actors and the Inuktitut language feature in it.

questions.description: Some people iron their shirts; some people iron their grass.
questions.question: A roller bends the grass one way and then the other to make them, and blades leaning away from you look lighter. Wimbledon's groundstaff are proud of theirs. What are they?
hints: You see them right after the grass has been mowed.
They make a lawn or a cricket pitch look neat and tidy.
They are bands of light and dark green, side by side.
questions.fun_fact: The grass in light and dark stripes is exactly the same colour; it only looks different because of how the blades catch the light.

questions.description: The vegetable that turns up at Christmas whether you invited it or not.
questions.question: I'm a small green ball of leaves. I'm served with Christmas dinner in Britain, and many children push me to the side of their plate. What am I?
hints: I grow in rows up a tall, thick stalk.
Cook me too long and I give off a strong smell.
I share my name with the capital city of Belgium.
questions.fun_fact: Brussels sprouts grow in spirals up a stalk that can be almost a metre tall.

questions.description: Norfolk's most famous feathered residents have a very busy diary.
questions.question: Aylesbury is to duck as Norfolk is to which bird?
hints: Before the railways, Norfolk farmers walked flocks of these birds all the way to London's markets.
A rare old breed of this bird is called the Norfolk Black.
Many British families roast one on 25 December.
questions.fun_fact: Before the railways, Norfolk turkeys were walked to the London markets in big flocks, a trip that could take weeks.

questions.question: Norfolk dumplings, nicknamed “swimmers”, leave out one ingredient that most British dumplings use. Which one?
hints: They were traditionally made from leftover bread dough.
The missing ingredient is a kind of hard fat.

questions.fun_fact: Norfolk cooks used up spare bread dough on baking day, so no dumpling ingredient went to waste.

hints: It's a tea-time loaf, sliced and buttered.

It's a pale dried grape.

hints: It's a body part most cats have, and most people would notice if it was missing.
Some Manx cats have only a short stub of it.
Other cats swish it when they are cross.

It shares its name with the island that England, Scotland and Wales are on.
questions.fun_fact: The ship came home to Bristol in 1970, almost exactly 127 years after it was launched in the same dock.

When the sea is in, the runway is underwater.
questions.fun_fact: Barra is said to be the only airport in the world where scheduled flights land on a beach.

hints: “Arr” is a country way of saying a very short word.
You might hear it from a farmer chatting over a pint in a village pub.
It's the opposite of “oh no”.
questions.fun_fact: Film pirates say “arr” partly thanks to Dorset-born actor Robert Newton, whose West Country growl as Long John Silver in 1950 set the style.

media.author: Lewis Clarke

questions.description: A place where people can say a lot by saying nowt at all.
questions.question: Here “nowt” means nothing, “owt” means anything, and a bread roll can be a “breadcake”. Which county are you in?
hints: It's in the north of England.
It's England's biggest county.
It shares its name with a pudding served with roast beef.
questions.fun_fact: An old Yorkshire saying goes: “Hear all, see all, say nowt”.

media.credit: Trevor Littlewood · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Trevor Littlewood

questions.description: Shoes so simple they're basically a sock with ambition.
questions.question: Northerners call them “pumps”, the Welsh say “daps”, and their other name comes from the Plimsoll line painted on ships. What are they?
hints: You wear them on your feet.
Think of a school PE lesson long ago.
They have a thin rubber sole and a cloth top.
questions.fun_fact: In Scotland they're often “sannies”, and in Northern Ireland “gutties”, from the gutta-percha rubber once used for soles.

media.credit: Czeva · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Czeva

questions.description: An actor whose vowels went on a long fantasy journey and came back unchanged.
questions.question: Which Sheffield-born actor kept his Yorkshire accent as Boromir in “The Lord of the Rings” and as the soldier Richard Sharpe?
hints: He has played lots of soldiers and warriors.
He's a huge Sheffield United fan.
His surname is also a vegetable.
questions.fun_fact: Sean Bean has a Sheffield United tattoo that reads “100% Blade”.

media.credit: Stephen Craven · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Stephen Craven

questions.description: A city where 18 degrees counts as a heatwave and a T-shirt counts as optional.
questions.question: People shout “taps aff”, meaning “tops off”, the moment the sun comes out. Which city's slang is it most famously linked with?
hints: It's not in England.
The words in the phrase are Scots, not standard English.
Its football teams include Celtic and Rangers.
questions.fun_fact: Glasgow is the biggest city in the UK outside England.

media.author: Paul Sableman

questions.description: A word so handy that people in the Valleys use it twice in a row.
questions.question: In the South Wales Valleys, people cry “Duw, duw!” when amazed, borrowing a word from Welsh. What does “Duw” mean?
hints: People say it to show surprise, but also sympathy.
It's a very important word in chapels and in Welsh hymns.
English speakers might say “Good Lord!” in the same moment.
questions.fun_fact: Wenglish speakers also say “now in a minute”, which means some time soon… probably.

questions.description: A meal so confusing that half the country turns up at the wrong time.
questions.question: In three of these cities, most people call their evening meal “tea”. Which is the odd one out, where most call it “dinner”?
hints: Which word you use depends a lot on where you grew up.
For many people, “dinner” is the meal you eat at midday.
It's the only southern city in the list.
questions.fun_fact: That's why school “dinner ladies” serve lunch: dinner was once the main meal in the middle of the day.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Ducks across the Midlands are tired of turning round for nothing.
questions.question: You'll hear it in Nottingham, Derby and Stoke, and the “duck” isn't a bird. What does “ay up me duck” mean?
hints: In this phrase, “me” simply means “my”.
“Me duck” is a friendly name, like “love”.
Bus drivers say it as you step on board.
questions.fun_fact: Using “duck” as a pet name is centuries old: in Shakespeare's “A Midsummer Night's Dream”, Pyramus cries “O dainty duck! O dear!”.

media.credit: Graham Robson · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Graham Robson

questions.description: Same person, different word, depending on which end of the country you grew up in.
questions.question: In Liverpool, Newcastle and Wales you call me “Mam”. I know your favourite tea, and I get cards on Mothering Sunday. Who am I?
hints: I probably remind you to brush your teeth.
In London, people use a slightly different word for me.
I'm your parent, but not your dad.
questions.fun_fact: British Mother's Day, or Mothering Sunday, falls in March or early April, not in May like in many other countries.

media.credit: Rodhullandemu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rodhullandemu

questions.description: A word that has echoed round the Tyne for generations.
questions.question: It's a Geordie word, you'll hear it at St James' Park, and fans chant it before “the lads”. What does “howay” mean?
hints: You say it to hurry someone up.
Fans shout it to push their team forward.
It's like saying “let's go!”.
questions.fun_fact: Sunderland fans usually spell it “Ha'way”, so the two rival cities even argue over spelling.

media.author: Benjamin Smith

questions.description: A kilt, a cartoon and almost no real Scots who actually say this.
questions.question: Complete the jokey Scottish phrase heard in countless films and cartoons: “Och aye the…”
hints: Comedians and cartoon Scots love saying this phrase.
In Scots, an “ow” sound often turns into “oo”, as in “hoose” for “house”.
It's the Scots way of saying “now”.
questions.fun_fact: “Och aye the noo” roughly means “oh yes, just now”, but it's mostly a joke version of Scottish speech.

questions.description: Yorkshire grandparents have a saying for everything, and this is one of the sharpest.
questions.question: In old Yorkshire, “Don't thee-tha me!” warned someone who had called you “thee” or “tha”. What were they being?
hints: “Thee” and “tha” are old forms of “you”, still heard in some Yorkshire dialect.
The saying was about who had the right to speak to you in a certain way.
“Thee” and “tha” were kept for close friends and family.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1600s, Quakers said “thee” and “thou” to everyone, even judges, to show that all people are equal.

hints: I'm from south London.
I set up a scholarship for Black students at Cambridge University.
My name sounds like bad weather.
questions.fun_fact: The Stormzy Scholarship, launched in 2018, pays tuition fees for Black British students at Cambridge.

media.author: Amakuru

questions.description: A small boy, a clay pipe, and one of the most successful soap sales in history.
questions.question: John Everett Millais's painting of a curly-haired boy gazing up at a soap bubble became a famous Pears soap advert. When did he paint it?
hints: It was painted in Queen Victoria's reign.
Millais painted it late in his life, some years before he died in 1896.
It was painted around the time of Victoria's Golden Jubilee in 1887.
questions.fun_fact: The boy was Millais's grandson, William James, who grew up to be an admiral and was teased with the nickname “Bubbles” for the rest of his life.

media.author: Bernard Gagnon

questions.description: A place where a stuntman jumped out of a helicopter and nobody called the police.
questions.question: In 2012, the Queen and James Bond seemed to parachute into it, and today West Ham play football there. Which stadium is it?
hints: It was built for a big sports event held in the UK in 2012.
It's in Stratford, in east London.
It was the main stadium of the 2012 Olympic Games.
questions.fun_fact: The seats can be moved: they slide over the running track to bring football fans closer to the pitch.

media.author: Jiří Sedláček

questions.description: The poster that stayed calm and carried on in a cupboard for sixty years.
questions.question: You've seen “Keep Calm and Carry On” on mugs and tea towels. Roughly how many copies of the original poster were printed in 1939?
hints: The government printed it for the whole country in case of war.
It was far more than one per town, but far fewer than one per person.
Think of millions, but just a handful of them.
questions.fun_fact: Hardly any were ever put up; the poster was forgotten until a copy turned up in a box of old books at Barter Books in Alnwick in 2000.

questions.description: A man with a lantern knocking at a door that has no handle on the outside.
questions.question: This famous Victorian painting, “The Light of the World”, hangs in Oxford and St Paul's Cathedral. Who painted it?
hints: The painter was one of the founders of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood.
He travelled to the Holy Land several times to paint Bible scenes.
He also painted “The Scapegoat”, a lone goat by the Dead Sea.
questions.fun_fact: The door in the painting has no handle, because the artist meant it can only be opened from the inside.

media.author: William Holman Hunt

questions.description: Named after not one, not two, not three, but four kings in a row, all with the same name.
questions.question: I'm a style of tall, neat brick or stone houses with sash windows and a fanlight over the door, named after four kings in a row. What am I?
hints: I was popular in the 1700s and early 1800s.
Bath's Royal Crescent is a famous example of me.
The four kings all shared one name, the same as England's patron saint.
questions.fun_fact: Georgian builders loved perfect symmetry so much that some houses have fake windows painted on, just to keep the front even.

questions.answer: Who was on the throne when it was put up
wrong_answers: Which postcode area it belongs to

What time the post is collected
hints: They have nothing to do with the post itself.
Two postboxes built in different decades can have different letters.

Actors perform there for the whole country, as its name suggests.
